https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-russia-tra.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IzY2 Ukrainian officials reported 10 dead and 18 wounded in Pechenihy in the Kharkiv region Image: Ukrainian Emergency Service/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Ukraine and Russia traded more attacks overnight, with the Kharkiv regional governor reporting 10 dead civilians not far from the Russian border and the Moscow mayor saying Ukraine launched some 620 drones toward the region. This follows one of the largest Ukrainian attacks on Russia during the war over the weekend , and the UN warning that amplified Russian strikes on towns and cities in July meant that civilian deaths in the conflict rose to levels not seen since May 2022 and the earliest months of combat. The drone attacks on the Moscow area again caused minor damage at a facility belonging to Russian online retail giant Wildberries, a frequent target for Ukrainian forces of late . Rescuers responded to the Tuesday morning missile strike near Ukraine's northeastern border to Russia Image: Ukrainian Emergency Service/AP Photo/picture alliance What happened in the Kharkiv missile strike? The governor of the Kharkiv oblast, Oleh Syniehubov, on Tuesday said that the 10 people were killed and 18 more wounded in a Russian missile strike on the village of Pechenihy. "The strike damaged 10 private houses, a cafe, a post office, a shop and at least seven cars," Syniehubov wrote on Telegram, noting that the casualty figures were preliminary. He said emergency services were responding and dealing with the attack. Parts of the Kharkiv region in northeastern Ukraine are occupied by Russian forces. Both Kharkiv and the Belgorod region across the border in Russia have been targeted frequently throughout the war. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack targeted a busy intersection. How Ukraine fights in the Black Sea without a navy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What happened as hundreds of drones approached Moscow? Moscow's Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Tuesday that some 620 drones had flown towards the capital region overnight. He said that most were intercepted on approach, and another 180 were shot down over the Moscow area. Moscow's regional governor posted an image of what he said was a fire at a construction site after a drone attack near Russia's capital Image: Moscow Region Governor Andrei Vorobyov's official telegram channel/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Russian state news agency TASS called it the heaviest such attack in two years. Russia's Defense Ministry said that, in total, it repelled 791 Ukrainian drones overnight across Russian territoy and the annexed Crimean Peninsula. The figures cannot be verified but indicate the intensity of Ukrainian strikes into Russian territory in recent days. Moscow's regional governor, Andrei Vorobyov, issued more details on the damage caused by the drones shot down over the capital, giving a slightly lower figure of "over 150." He said that three people were injured in three separate districts, including a young girl with a shrapnel wound to the hand. Vorobyov also reported damage to several mainly residential buildings, including one house that "burned down completely in the village of Kuznetsy." He said that a drone also struck a "Wildberries warehouse near Atlant-Park" in the city of Kolomna, which also logged damage at a retail site near a shopping center. Russian court confirms anti-war party election ban To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did Russia say about reports of UK drones being used in strikes on its territory? Russia's Embassy in London also turned its attention to drone attacks this week, responding critically on Monday evening to reports in newspaper The Times saying that drones supplied by the UK had been used in attacks on Russian territory. The embassy asserted that such reports "confirm that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis, while hypocritically professing a desire for peace." It accused the UK of "acting as an accomplice and co-perpetrator of the bloody crimes and terrorist attacks committed by Ukrainian neo-Nazis," and said that "London's actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer." What did Germany's environment minister say during his visit to Kyiv? Also on Tuesday, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider traveled to Kyiv . The Social Democrat (SPD) politician planned to spend several days in the country this week if circumstances allow. "The goal of the trip is to work with our Ukrainian partners to identify, at an early stage, opportunities for a climate-friendly, resilient renewal of infrastructure and further reconstruction, including with the participation of the German business community," the Envirnoment Ministry said on Tuesday as Schneider was arriving. The minister was accompanied by business representatives, not least from companies specializing in climate-friendly technologies. Schneider also planned to be briefed on the situation for Ukraine's nuclear power plants, including the damage to protective dome covering the Chernobyl or Chornobyl reactor that melted down in the 1980s during the Soviet era. "Its repair is highly complex," the ministry said. Ukraine's main functioning nuclear power plant at Zaporizhzhia , meanwhile, has been under Russian military occupation and operational control since the first weeks of the war in 2022. Its reactors are in cold shutdown status but the plant still requires external power, cooling and maitenance. Close to the front lines, the plant and the surrounding area has fairly frequently come under fire. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Elizabeth Struhs died from diabetic ketoacidosis in 2022 after her parents and other sect members withdrew her insulin. Photograph: BBC View image in fullscreen Elizabeth Struhs died from diabetic ketoacidosis in 2022 after her parents and other sect members withdrew her insulin. Photograph: BBC Queensland Doctor warned Elizabeth Struhs would not be safe years before sect killed her by withdrawing medicine Inquest hears paediatricians pleaded with child safety for action to protect the eight-year-old from her parents and other Toowoomba sect members Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Andrew Messenger Mon 12 Oct 2026 07.28 EDT First published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 02.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A specialist child safety doctor was “stonewalled” by a child safety officer after repeatedly warning that Elizabeth Struhs would not be safe living with her mother, years before her parents allowed her to die by withdrawing lifesaving medicine, a coronial inquest has heard. Elizabeth returned to live with her parents at her family home in Toowoomba in 2019, after both of them were convicted of neglecting her. The type 1 diabetic died there on 7 January 2022 from diabetic ketoacidosis, after they and other members of their religious sect withdrew the insulin she needed to survive. All 14 adult members of the sect, known as the Saints, were convicted of her manslaughter last year, including her father, Jason Struhs, mother, Kerrie Struhs, and brother, Zachary Struhs, and the leader of their sect, Brendan Stevens. The group, which some have referred to as “a cult” , did not believe in medicine, and believed Elizabeth would be miraculously healed of her incurable illness and be resurrected after she died. They sat singing and praying while she slowly died over the course of several days. Elizabeth had been hospitalised in 2019 after a similar incident left her in a coma and on a ventilator after being taken to intensive care in Brisbanefrom the Toowoomba hospital. 5:49 Fourteen members of religious sect found guilty of killing eight-year-old Elizabeth Struhs - video The inquest, which began in Brisbane on Monday, heard the department of child safety had been alerted to the family’s extreme religious beliefs as early as 2013, after another child fled the family. The coroner, Ainslie Kirkegaard, heard from two senior paediatricians working in the Queensland children’s hospital who raised the alarm after the 2019 incident. They cannot be identified for legal reasons. Both put their concerns in writing repeatedly. They told the inquest they were worried about Elizabeth’s very poor condition and her mother’s extreme religious beliefs. Counsel assisting, Simon Hamlyn-Harris, read from a nine-page report written by another doctor the day after Elizabeth’s admission to the Queensland children’s hospital, which was sent to child safety and the police. “‘Type 1 diabetes is a life-threatening condition that requires complicated care by the parents’, the report reads,” he said. “‘If her mother continues to deny the requirement for insulin and the related treatments Elizabeth could not be in Kerrie’s care’. “With ‘not’ in bold,” Hamlyn-Harris added. Another email he read said Elizabeth “cannot safely be cared for in a home where her mother resides due to the strong beliefs that she’s expressing”. The entire section was underlined and bolded. In a phone conversation with one doctor, Kerrie refused to attend the hospital to see her child, and denied that she was sick or would ever require medication, the court was told. Kerrie did not ask any questions about her daughter’s condition, the doctor said. In an email sent at the time and read in court on Monday, the other doctor made a clinical assessment that Kerrie was “delusional” and recommended she receive a mental health assessment. “Even now mum is expecting divine intervention and insulin is unnecessary. Elizabeth was minutes away from death,” the email read. If Elizabeth lived with her “the risk is too high”, it read. The doctor described Kerrie’s perspective about her daughter’s condition as “chilling”. She attended a meeting with a child safety officer to urge for additional protection but was given the impression they could not intervene because Elizabeth’s father, Jason, was willing to assist her to treat her diabetes. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “I felt I was expressing my concerns, but I actually felt stonewalled by it,” the doctor told the inquest. “It’s not common that I feel that way when I’m communicating with child safety.” The doctor was later not invited to a subsequent suspected child abuse and neglect team meeting about Elizabeth, despite asking to attend, she said. The doctor blamed a poor relationship with the Toowoomba hospital and health service for a lack of consensus on the best approach to keep Elizabeth safe. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Elizabeth was ultimately returned home to live with her family, with an intervention parental agreement: a short-term, voluntary, intensive arrangement which allows child safety authorities to aid a child in danger without a child protection order, the inquest heard. The inquest heard the plan put the onus on Elizabeth to “essentially protect herself by identifying if she feels unwell”, one of the two doctors said. “Putting the onus on Elizabeth is not an appropriate thing to do for a six-year-old child in this environment,” she said. “Elizabeth can become extremely unwell in a matter of hours without appropriate care of her diabetes,” a 2019 email read. One doctor described herself as “distressed” about the situation, and told the coroner she believed she had exhausted every available pathway to report her concerns. Elizabeth’s father, Jason, agreed to care for Elizabeth after her discharge from hospital, which he did for three years. At the time, Jason was a longtime sceptic of his wife’s religion, and had saved Elizabeth’s life by taking her to hospital against the wishes of his wife in 2019 and then testified against her at a criminal trial. Both Jason and Kerrie were found guilty in 2021 of failing to supply the necessaries of life for their daughter, relating to the incident in 2019 which was so serious Elizabeth was taken to hospital in a coma. Jason was sentenced to six months in prison, wholly suspended for a period of 12 months, while Kerrie was sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment with a specified parole release date of 15 December 2021. But Kerrie helped convert Jason to her religious beliefs while serving her prison sentence. He was then convinced to give up treating Elizabeth’s diabetes with insulin, leading to her death. The inquest continues. https://www.politico.eu/article/northern.text: Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant rejected furious accusations from the U.K. region’s unionists Monday that he had “bent the knee” to Irish republicans blocking a long-disputed Protestant march. Bryant told the House of Commons that his decision to ban what had been a legally authorized parade by the Orange Order — a pro-British Protestant brotherhood reviled by many of Northern Ireland’s Catholics — had been taken principally to avoid violence. Thousands led by Sinn Fein, the main Irish republican party, had spent nearly two weeks blocking the Orangemen’s intended path down the Garvaghy Road, the main Catholic district in the town of Portadown, but police kept the two sides apart. “The Orange Order obtained a legal right to parade, but … upholding the determination does not come at any cost. Upholding the law also means judiciously preventing serious disorder,” Bryant said in defense of his intervention Friday night . Advertisement Advertisement Democratic Unionist leader Gavin Robinson accused Bryant of bowing to a threat of violence from Irish Republican Army militants who featured prominently within the Garvaghy Road crowd. Most IRA members have observed a cease-fire since 1997 and officially disarmed in 2005, but several small factions still plot occasional bomb and gun attacks. Robinson said Northern Ireland’s unionists “know that this British government has bent the knee to them.” But Bryant said his decision to bar the Orangemen — despite a decision last month by the region’s independent Parades Commission to permit a heavily restricted march by 35 Orangemen — had so far kept violence at bay. “I utterly reject the charge that I have in any way succumbed to mob rule. The truth is, things have actually passed remarkably peacefully,” he said, adding: “I don’t think anybody seriously proposed that the police should drag people off the street.” He spoke hours after two courts in Northern Ireland tangled with the conflict of rights stirred up by the revival of the Orange marching demands in Portadown, a sectarian dispute that triggered bloodshed and rioting across Northern Ireland in the mid-1990s. The Court of Appeal, overseen by Northern Ireland’s highest judge, rejected a lawsuit by the Garvaghy Road protesters seeking to challenge the original Parades Commission ruling. Orange supporters said this judgment kept the door open for an eventual parade down Garvaghy Road for the first time since 1997, when police backed by British soldiers forced the parade through with the use of armored vehicles and volleys of plastic bullets. Advertisement Advertisement A separate Belfast High Court hearing gave the go-ahead for Portadown’s Orange lodge to pursue a legal challenge against both Bryant and Northern Ireland’s police commander, Chief Constable Jon Boutcher. That case will be heard starting next Monday. Boutcher, rejecting unionist calls for him to resign, issued his own lengthy defense of his officers’ management of the Portadown standoff. He appealed to both sides to respect a legal process that could take months to conclude — including potential charges against senior Sinn Féin figures involved in the Garvaghy Road blockade. The legal fight over whose rights should prevail is fracturing Northern Ireland’s cross-community government, a bitterness on full display Monday night at Stormont, the center of government on a hill overlooking Belfast. After a three-hour debate in the Northern Ireland Assembly, unionist members voted unanimously to oust the four Sinn Féin ministers from their supposed unity government. Unionists accused all four, led by First Minister Michelle O’Neill , of breaking their ministerial pledge to uphold the law of the land by joining and encouraging the Garvaghy Road protests. O’Neill accused her accusers on the other side of the chamber of being reactionary bigots. “It’s no surprise to me that the three unionist parties have signed up to this motion. They have never accepted the reality that an Irish republican is now the first minister, and a woman at that. They have never accepted equality,” she said. Advertisement Advertisement The unionists’ motion of no confidence bore no legal weight because of Stormont’s peculiar power-sharing rules. This would have required Sinn Féin members to join the unionists in voting to punish their own leaders. In the end, four motions — seeking the expulsion from office for a year of O’Neill, Finance Minister John O’Dowd, Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald and Infrastructure Minister Liz Kimmins — all failed on virtually identical sectarian tests. While 33 to 34 unionists voted to kick out each one, 35 lawmakers from Sinn Féin and a smaller Irish nationalist party, the SDLP, voted to keep them in office. O’Neill’s official co-leader of Northern Ireland’s four-party government, Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly of the Democratic Unionists, said she understood the law as a barrister — and her government colleague had broken it by leading a “mob” that included well-known figures from multiple IRA factions “threatening violence and disorder.”

Contributed / Laura Migliorino By Theo Babb September 30, 2026 at 9:00 AM Listen Comments Share Share this article News Reporting News Reporting Based on facts, either observed and verified firsthand by the reporter, or reported and verified from knowledgeable sources. The Trust Project What is this? WORTHINGTON — Since April, white painted shoes have been popping up around Minnesota in areas where ICE agents have killed, taken or simply hurt residents. As of two weeks ago, the Ghost Shoes have made it to Worthington. Two pairs were placed in Worthington, one set near U.S. 59 and another near Omaha Avenue, where ICE made warrantless arrests earlier this year. ADVERTISEMENT They’re part of a public art project by Laura Migliorino, a Twin Cities-based artist. Ghost Shoes have popped up in Worthington as part of a public art project. Contributed / Laura Migliorino “A lot of my own work deals with history and memory, so, my response to (ICE activity) was immediately ‘Remembrance,’” Migliorino explained. “How do we mark this? How do we remember it?” She began brainstorming the project when Forecast Public Art, a St. Paul non-profit, put out a call for “Artists as Witness” in January, offering grants to artists who were “bearing witness.” “(I) came up with Ghost Shoes (as) a way of marking where somebody died, was kidnapped, harmed, traumatized by an ICE agent or ICE action,” Migliorino said. “(I) was combining Holocaust memorials that I have seen, particularly one in Budapest (and) Ghost Bikes that you see where somebody died on a bicycle.” The Budapest memorial she’s referring to is “The Shoes on the Danube Bank,” a row of bronze shoes in downtown Budapest where thousands of victims, primarily Jews, were lined up along the Danube River and shot by Hungarian fascists during World War II. “(There’s) all these bronze shoes of different (kinds), kids and women and men, different kinds of shoes,” Migliorino said. “Expressing that wide range of different kinds of people who were murdered at that moment.” Migliorino explained that she finds shoes incredibly poignant, heightened with phrases like “Walk in somebody’s shoes” or “Stand in somebody’s shoes.” ADVERTISEMENT “Shoes are personal. They're intimate,” Migliorino said. She began collecting shoes and painting them with white outdoor house paint. The paint stiffens the shoes and makes them unwearable. “I tag them, do all the processing, put them in a box and ship them out to the volunteers.” Migliorino found artists throughout the state, whether they were colleagues, friends or just names pulled from the state art department’s directory, and asked them to be a part of the project. Shoes were shipped off and then hung up by those willing. PEOPLE Worthington Middle, High School choirs celebrate America’s 250th 3h ago Reel Life: 'A River Runs Through It' 4h ago Ocheda Orchard’s Chuck Nystrom shares story behind SugarBee apple 1d ago Initially, the project was just in the Twin Cities, but Migliorino knew that ICE’s impact reached much farther than the city she lived in. “Minneapolis kind of floated to the top of the news cycle, (but) southern Minnesota got hit hard, really hard. I wanted to have the whole state sharing that acknowledgment and that remembrance.” A second grant, this time from Springboard For The Arts, was applied for and granted, allowing Migliorino to spread the project beyond the Twin Cities. The goal is 100 sets of Ghost Shoes placed around the state. ADVERTISEMENT “I want the shoes here to be tended, to remain,” Migliorino said. “I want this to continue. I want, 10 years from now, somebody to see a white shoe and go, ‘Hmm, what's that?’” She’s in the process of finding funding to expand the project beyond Minnesota. More information can be found on the project’s website: iceghostshoes26.com.
